metaData.title: "Token Economy" Enters the Outcome Layer
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article deeply analyzes the evolution of AI pricing models from per-token/call volume to pay-per-outcome, using Intercom's Fin, which charges $0.99 per resolved customer issue, as a case study to explore four core issues of outcome-based pricing, applicable scenarios, and its implications for the Chinese market.
metaData.summary: This article is the 11th installment of the "Token Economics" series, focusing on a key shift in AI software business models: from selling accounts and API calls to selling "completed tasks." Using Intercom's AI customer service bot Fin, which charges $0.99 per resolved customer issue, as a starting point, the article systematically deconstructs four core issues behind the "pay-per-outcome" model: how to define "completion," how to prove contribution, how to calculate costs, and how to allocate responsibility. The author points out that outcome-based AI will make software "heavier" because it requires integrating processes, tools, rules, and verification mechanisms, evolving from a toolbox into an execution system. The article also analyzes the applicable boundaries of this model (high-frequency, clearly defined boundaries, verifiable outcomes) and its unique path in the Chinese market, which may initially appear in non-standardized forms like project-based contracts or performance-based payments. Finally, the article connects the three pricing layers of Token, Action, and Outcome, noting that the price tag is shifting from "paying for capability" to a "list of responsibilities."

mainPoints.point: AI pricing is evolving from per-token/call volume to pay-per-outcome, with Intercom's Fin as a typical case.
mainPoints.explanation: Fin charges $0.99 per resolved customer issue, not per conversation or token consumption, marking a shift for AI software from selling tools to selling completed work.

mainPoints.point: Pay-per-outcome requires solving four core issues: defining completion, proving contribution, calculating costs, and allocating responsibility.
mainPoints.explanation: The boundary of 'completion' varies by scenario, requiring logs and process records to prove AI's contribution. Cost calculation involves complexities like multiple issues or handoffs to humans, and responsibility attribution is key to determining if AI can truly become a 'supplier.'

mainPoints.point: Outcome-based AI will make software 'heavier,' evolving from a toolbox into an execution system.
mainPoints.explanation: Committing to outcome delivery requires integrating infrastructure like knowledge bases, ticketing systems, and approval workflows. AI acts more like a general contractor than a single tool, needing a deep understanding of industry processes and rules.

mainPoints.point: Applicable scenarios for pay-per-outcome require conditions like high frequency, clear boundaries, verifiable outcomes, and controllable risks.
mainPoints.explanation: Scenarios like customer service, content moderation, and reconciliation are better suited for outcome-based pricing than strategic consulting or investment due diligence. The difficulty lies not in AI capability but in designing the transaction structure.

mainPoints.point: The Chinese market may initially adopt project-based contracts and performance-based payments rather than standardized price pages.
mainPoints.explanation: Chinese companies tend to embed outcome-based fees within sales and delivery contracts, which can slow the diffusion of this new pricing model. The transition from project to product is a key watershed.

keyQuotes: What is being sold is shifting from 'you can use this' to 'this task has been completed.'
Token is the underlying cost, Action is the business step, and Outcome is the completed deliverable that can be paid for.
When the pricing model for AI shifts from 'paying for capability' to 'paying for completion,' the price tag of AI software increasingly resembles a 'list of responsibilities.'

Outcome-based AI is more like a general contractor: it doesn't necessarily produce every part, but it must organize people, processes, tools, rules, and verification to ultimately deliver a piece of work that can be signed off on.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Is Not the Goal, Knowledge Is the Moat — Knowledge Accumulation Practices of an AI Engineering Delivery Team
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the engineering delivery practices of an AI Team, this article proposes that knowledge accumulation is more important than workflow orchestration, and systematically introduces a complete methodology encompassing a five-layer knowledge storage architecture, a three-level maturity system, and how workflows serve knowledge accumulation.

relatedArticles.title: Why Did Hermes Take Over from OpenClaw in Just Two Months?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth comparison between the rising open-source AI Agent star Hermes and its predecessor OpenClaw, arguing that Hermes' success stems not from functional superiority but from encapsulating decision complexity—such as skill auto-evolution and proactive memory management—within underlying deterministic rules. This engineering safety net allowed it to deliver an automated 'gets better with use' experience precisely when the underlying technology was just barely sufficient.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Hermes in One Article: How the New Top-Tier Agent Self-Evolves from Experience
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the core innovation of the Hermes Agent—the Skills closed-loop system—detailing its complete implementation mechanism, from experience extraction and knowledge storage to intelligent retrieval and self-improvement, along with its engineering trade-offs and security considerations.

relatedArticles.title: A Serious Discussion: How Much of Our Skills Can Skill Actually Distill? | Hao's Trend Talk
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article delves into the capability boundaries of AI Agent Skills, pointing out that while they excel at encoding explicit rules and knowledge routing, they cannot capture the tacit intuition and utility judgment that human experts rely on in complex decision-making.

relatedArticles.title: Q1 2026: AI Agents Come of Age | 2026 Q1 AI Trend White Paper
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of four structural trends in AI Agents for Q1 2026: long-horizon productization, harness engineering, recursive R&D, and the Skill ecosystem, revealing the flywheel effect as Agents evolve from tools into independent 'new colleagues'.

relatedArticles.title: The Evolution of Agent/Skills/Teams Architectures and Principles of Technology Selection
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically reviews the evolutionary trajectory of AI Agents from monolithic to multi-agent, then to Skills pluginization and Teams parallel collaboration, and, drawing on the latest research from Google and Anthropic, provides a scientific methodology for selection.

relatedArticles.title: What You Don't Know About Claude Code: Architecture, Governance, and Engineering Practices - Tw93
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of Claude Code's six-layer architecture and engineering practices, proposing a systematic Agent development methodology from context governance and skill design to a verification loop.

relatedArticles.title: Investing 10,000 RMB in AI: A Year of Tools, Practices, and Reflections
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A systematic summary of a veteran developer's practical experience in the AI wave, covering everything from MAC toolchain optimization and Harness Engineering architectural constraints to building an Agent-driven automated learning loop.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Harness Engineering: Finding the Shell That Keeps AI from Going Rogue—Insights from 14 Engineering Articles | Hao's Trend Talk
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of "Harness Engineering," a core technology in the AI Agent field. It reveals how to compensate for model shortcomings through a three-layer management architecture and proposes the logic of "Compensation Surface Migration" that evolves with model capabilities.

relatedArticles.title: In the AI-Induced Cognitive Disarmament, We Will Lose More Than Just Ability | Hao Chat on Trends
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: From the perspectives of cognitive psychology, labor sociology, and philosophy, this article systematically argues that the 'cognitive disarmament' brought about by AI is not a simple degradation of abilities, but a historic turning point where alienation has deepened from the labor process to the thought generation process, rooted in the growth society's endless pursuit of efficiency.
